summary:
Haiti has not criminalised same-sex conduct since 1791. Its legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement, and the judiciary does not function in practice as a protection avenue. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory remedy to invoke and no aggravated-penalty framework standing behind a complaint.

Two Senate measures would tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Mœurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017, and this record documents no later legislative outcome.

A 2018 US State Department report found that attitudes in Haiti remained hostile toward LGBTI people who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. The report is the most recent official climate assessment carried in this record, and no later assessment is sourced here.

Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019. An LGBTQ news outlet reported that he may have been poisoned, a finding it could not confirm, and ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. The most recent documented death of this kind in this record is dated 2019; no later instance is documented.

Transgender people face documented harassment in the displacement camps that followed the 2010 earthquake. No later instance of camp-based harassment appears in this record, and no prevalence figure is sourced for it.

Constitutional guarantees of health care, housing, education, food and social security extend to citizens, so a trans visitor cannot invoke them. After the 2010 earthquake, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanor to avoid harassment and to reduce the chance of being denied emergency housing, healthcare and food-for-work programs; no later disaster-response evidence appears in this record.
tangentialFactors:
Health context is documented only to older dates: HIV infection rates in Haiti rose to 4-6% as of 2008, with 13% recorded in certain rural neighborhoods. These are general-population figures, not a trans-specific measure, and the record supplies no more recent epidemiological baseline for a visitor who needs HIV-related care.

The record contains no comparative positioning for Haiti against other jurisdictions and no trans-specific violence rate expressed against a denominator. Its violence documentation consists of individual named incidents rather than counted or ranked data, so no per-capita or cross-country inference can be drawn from it.

Statements in the record come from external monitors: an international human-rights organisation's 2018 country chapter, a foreign government's 2018 report, and a regional LGBTQ rights group's public mourning. Haiti's own institutions are not documented as issuing guidance for trans travellers.
localsOnly:
The Certificat de Bonne Vie et Mœurs, required by many employers and schools, lists homosexuality as a crime that can justify denial of the certificate, which bears directly on young people and students. In June 2017 the Senate launched a bill to regulate who receives the certification, and the broader June 2017 measure would permit denial on grounds of homosexuality.

LGBTQ people in Haiti often conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity for fear of discrimination, and that concealment impedes access to services otherwise guaranteed. The 1987 Constitution guarantees all citizens a right to education, while LGBTQ youth face pervasive social hostility in practice.

Community organisations work on health among LGBTQ Haitians: Grasadis, founded in 1997, focuses on preventing the spread of HIV/AIDS within the LGBTQ minority. The HIV prevalence figures available in this record date from 2008.

The August 2017 Senate bill on marriage and public advocacy, with its three-year maximum term and fine of about US$8,000, would fall on residents and organisers rather than on visitors, and it remained pending before the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017.
outOfScopeNotes:
Custody and prison placement for trans detainees are unresolved in this source set. No rule assigning housing by birth sex or by identity is documented, no separate units for trans prisoners are recorded, and no solitary-confinement or segregation practice appears in the record.

Whether either 2017 Senate bill progressed past the Chamber of Deputies after November 2017 is not sourced here; the record stops at that date.

The cause of Charlot Jeudy's death on 25 November 2019 is unresolved: poisoning was reported but not confirmed, and no subsequent official finding is carried in the record.

No survey of trans people in Haiti, with a stated category and period, appears in the source set. The 2018 discrimination assessment is an international human-rights organisation's general finding about LGBT people, not a current trans-specific prevalence measure.

Nothing in the record addresses gender markers on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening of trans travellers, or airport and border treatment linked to gender presentation.
